en: The Gorakṣa-śataka. Oṃ, salutations to the supreme guru, Gorakṣanātha.
Oṃ, I shall proclaim the Gorakṣa-śataka for the sake of liberation from the bonds of worldly existence.
It brings about self-realization for men and serves as the key to the door of discernment. (Gorakṣaśataka 1)
This is the ladder to liberation, this is the deception of Time:
that the mind, having turned away from delusion, is attached to the Supreme Self. (Gorakṣaśataka 2)

The virtuous person practices yoga, which is the fruit of the wish-fulfilling tree of the Vedas— whose branches are frequented by the twice-born— and which brings about the pacification of the suffering of worldly existence.
Posture, restraint of breath, withdrawal of the senses, concentration, meditation, and absorption—these are the six limbs of yoga. (Gorakṣaśataka 4)
There are as many postures as there are species of living beings;
Maheśvara knows all their various distinctions. (Gorakṣa-śataka 5)
Each one of the eighty-four lakhs has been proclaimed;
thereafter, Śiva established one hundred and sixteen sacred seats (pīṭhas).
Among all postures, only two are distinguished:
one is declared to be Siddhāsana, and the second is Kamalāsana. (Gorakṣaśataka 7)

Having firmly placed the root of one foot against the perineum (yoni-sthānaka), and having made the body steady and level, one should remain motionless with the senses restrained; looking between the eyebrows with a fixed gaze, this is called Siddhāsana, which effects the breaking open of the door to liberation. (Gorakṣaśataka 8)

Having placed the right foot upon the left thigh and likewise the left foot upon the right thigh, holding them firmly with both hands according to the prescribed method, and placing the two big toes at the heart, one should gaze at the tip of the nose; this is called the *padmāsana* of the self-restrained, which removes the transformations of disease. (Gorakṣaśataka 9)
The Foundation (ādhāra) is the first wheel, and the Self-Abiding (svādhiṣṭhāna) is the second;
situated between these two is the Yoni-place, which is called Kāmarūpa.

In the place called the *ādhāra*, located at the anus, there is a four-petalled lotus; in its center is said to be the womb (*yoni*) named Kāmā, which is worshipped by the perfected ones (*siddhas*). (GorS 1.11)
He who knows that the great liṅga stands within the womb facing west, split like a jewel at its crown, is a knower of yoga. (GorS 1.12)
Resembling molten gold and flashing like a streak of lightning, the quadrangular city of Fire is designated as the lower penis (adho-meḍhra). (GorS 1.13)
By its own name it is *prāṇa*, and its support is the *svādhiṣṭhāna*;
therefore, by the designation "svādhiṣṭhāna," the penis itself is denoted. (Gorakṣaśataka 14)
Where the *kanda* is strung like a gem upon a thread by means of the *suṣumṇā*, that navel-center is called the *maṇipūraka-cakra*. (Gorakṣaśataka 15)
Above the penis and below the navel is the source of the kanda, like its own bulbous root;
from there, seventy-two thousand channels have arisen.
Among those thousands of channels, seventy-two are declared to be primary;
among them, ten are traditionally held to be the principal carriers of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Iḍā and Piṅgalā, and Suṣumṇā as the third;
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, Pūṣā, and Yaśasvinī. (Gorakṣa Śataka 18)
Alambuṣā, Kuhū, and Śaṅkhinī is remembered as the tenth;
this wheel consisting of channels should always be known by yogins. (GorS 1.19)
The iḍā is situated on the left side, and likewise the piṅgalā on the right;
the suṣumṇā is in the middle region, while the gāndhārī is in the left eye.
On the right is Hastijihvā and Pūṣā on the right ear;
Yaśasvinī is on the left ear, and Alambuṣā is also on the seat.
Kūhū is at the region of the *liṅga*, and Śaṅkhinī is at the root-place;
thus, ten channels remain stationed, having taken recourse to the gateway.
The three channels that constantly carry the vital breath, presided over by the deities Soma, Sūrya, and Agni, are declared to be Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumṇā. (Gorakṣaśataka 23)
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
as well as nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya.

The five well-known [winds] beginning with Nāga and the five vital airs (vāyu) beginning with Prāṇa—these, existing in the form of the individual soul (jīva), circulate within the thousands of channels (nāḍī). 25.
The living soul, under the sway of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, runs upward and downward;
because of its flickering nature, it is not perceived through the left and right channels.
Just as a ball thrown upon the ground rises up when struck by a stick,
so too is the living soul drawn along, impelled by the vital breaths (prāṇa) and the downward breath (apāna).
Just as a hawk tied with a rope is pulled back even though it has flown away,
so too the individual soul (jīva), bound by the qualities (guṇas), is drawn along by the out-breath and in-breath.
The apāna draws up the prāṇa, and the prāṇa draws up the apāna;
he who knows these two as situated above and below is a knower of yoga.
Above the *kanda*, the power of Kuṇḍalinī is coiled eightfold;
she stands eternally covering the entrance of the gate of Brahman with her mouth. (Gorakṣaśataka 30)
Awakened by the yoga of fire and struck by the mind, the breath,
having taken up the quality of the individual soul, ascends through the *suṣumṇā*.
He who knows Mahāmudrā, the mudrā of salutation, Oḍḍiyāna, Jālandhara, and Mūlabandha—that yogi is a vessel for accomplishment. (Gorakṣaśataka 32)

Placing the chin upon the chest, pressing the vulva for a long time with the left foot, and likewise holding the extended right foot with both hands, one should fill the two sides of the abdomen with breath and slowly exhale; this is declared to be the great *mudrā* of men, which destroys all sins. (Gorakṣaśataka 33)
When the tongue enters the hollow of the skull and moves in reverse, and the gaze is fixed between the eyebrows, that becomes the Khecarī Mudrā. (Gorakṣaśataka 34)
That which is above the penis and below the navel is called Uḍḍiyāna;
the mastery of Uḍḍiyāna is the Bandha that is a lion to the elephant of death. (Gorakṣaśataka 35)
When the Jālandhara lock, characterized by the constriction of the throat, is performed, the nectar does not fall into the fire, nor does the vital wind become disturbed. (Gorakṣaśataka 36)
Pressing with the heel, one should contract the perineum and the anus;
drawing the *apāna* upward, this is called the *mūla-bandha*. (Gorakṣaśataka 37)
Since Brahmā, as well as yogins and sages, were devoted to breath control out of fear of time, one should therefore bind the vital breath.
When the wind moves, everything moves; when it is still, everything becomes still.
The yogi attains the state of a pillar; therefore, he should bind the vital air.
The *haṃsa* moves thirty-six finger-breadths outside through the left and right channels; therefore, it is designated as *prāṇa*. (Gorakṣaśataka 40)

The yogi, having assumed the bound lotus posture (baddha-padmāsana) and having paid homage to the Guru who is Śiva, should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma) alone, with his gaze fixed on the tip of the nose. (Gorakṣaśataka 41)
Life-force (*prāṇa*) is the wind situated within the body; *āyāma* is its restraint.
A measure (*mātrā*) consisting of a single breath—through that, the yogi becomes like the sky. (GorS 1.42)
The yogin, having assumed the bound lotus posture (baddha-padmāsana), should fill [the body] with breath through the moon;
having retained it according to his capacity, he should exhale again through the sun.

Having meditated upon the lunar orb, which resembles an ocean of nectar and possesses a radiance as white as the Ocean of Milk, one shall become happy through breath control (prāṇāyāma). (Gorakṣaśataka 44)
Having drawn in the vital breath through the sun, one should slowly fill the abdomen;
having retained it according to the rule, one should then exhale through the moon.
Having meditated upon the orb of the sun as a mass of blazing flames situated at the navel, the yogi shall become happy in the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma). (GorS 1.46)

Exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka) constitute the threefold breath control (prāṇāyāma) which is essentially the Praṇava; it is joined with twelve measures (mātrās). // GorS(1) 47 //
In the lowest [grade] of breath control, there are twelve measures; in the middling, twice that;
and in the highest, three times that—such is the determination regarding prāṇāyāma.
In the lowest [stage], there is perspiration and heat; in the middling, trembling occurs;
in the highest, the yogi repeatedly rises while seated in the bound lotus posture.
Massaging the limbs with water produced from physical exertion is recommended;
one should abandon pungent, sour, and salty foods and subsist on a diet of milk.
One should inhale the breath very slowly and release it very slowly;
one should not excessively restrain the breath, nor should one release it too quickly. (Gorakṣaśataka 51)
Having drawn up the downward-voiding wind (apāna), one should unite it with the vital breath (prāṇa);
by means of the power [of this practice], one is led to the crown of the head and is liberated from all sins.
Thus, breath control (prāṇāyāma) becomes the burner of the fuel of sins; it is always described by yogis as a great bridge across the ocean of transgressions. (GorS 1.53)
Through *āsana* the yogi destroys physical ailments, through *prāṇāyāma* he destroys sin, and through *pratyāhāra* he always destroys mental afflictions. (Gorakṣaśataka 54)
The sun draws back the stream consisting of lunar nectar;
that drawing back of it is called his "withdrawal" (pratyāhāra). (Gorakṣaśataka 55)
One woman is enjoyed by two who have come from the lunar orb;
he who is the third among them becomes free from old age and death.
In the region of the navel there exists one sun, whose nature is burning;
and at the root of the palate, the moon, whose nature is nectar, resides eternally.
When the moon rains while facing downward and the sun devours while facing upward, one must understand the method (*karaṇa*) therein by which nectar is obtained. (GorS 1.58)
The navel is above and the palate is below; the sun is above and the moon is below.
This practice known as "the reversal" is obtained from the mouth of the Guru.
Where the bull, bound in three ways, bellows with a great sound,
yogis know that to be the unstruck wheel (anāhata-cakra) in the heart.
Having transcended the unstruck sound (*anāhata*) and having passed through the *maṇipūra*,
when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) reaches the great lotus (*mahāpadma*), the state of a yogi becomes immortal.
The word *vi* is traditionally remembered as *haṃsa*; it is said to be stainless and pure.
Therefore, those who know the cakras recognize the cakra called Viśuddha in the throat. (GorS 1.62)
Having held the water of the lunar digit within the pure, supreme wheel,
one does not undergo depletion for a month, having deceived the mouth of the sun.
Having pressed the great cavity of the royal tooth with the tip of the tongue and meditated upon the Goddess consisting of nectar, one becomes a poet within six months.
For the yogin whose body is filled with nectar, after two or three years,
semen begins to flow, and the emergence of qualities such as *aṇimā* occurs.
Just as fire does not leave its fuel, nor a lamp its oil and wick,
so the embodied soul, filled with the digits of the moon, does not abandon the body.
Endowed with the proper posture, joined with breath control,
and joined with sensory withdrawal, one should practice concentration.
In the heart, the concentration on each of the five elements is performed individually,
and concentration is also prescribed through the immobility of the mind.

That which is the earth-element, beautiful like the land of Haritāla, yellow in color, marked with the letter *La*, conjoined with the Lotus-Seated One (Brahmā), and situated in the heart in the form of a quadrangle—one should fix the breath there for five *ghaṭikās* and maintain it together with the mind; this "earth-dhāraṇā" always causes immobilization and brings victory over the earth. (Gorakṣa Śataka 69)
The water-element (ambu-tattva) situated in the throat is like a half-moon, white as a jasmine flower, and joined with the seed-syllable *Vaṃ* which is like nectar; it is eternally united with Viṣṇu.

Having restrained the vital breath (*prāṇa*) there, one should hold it for five *ghaṭikās* with a concentrated mind. This is the *Vāriṇī* concentration, which digests even the most difficult-to-swallow *kālakūṭa* poison.

That reality which is situated at the palate, resembling an *indrāgopa* insect, radiant with its three angles, consisting of the syllable *ra* and the element of fire, beautiful as a coral sprout, and joined with Rudra—one should fix the breath there for five *ghaṭikās* along with the mind; this is the Vaiśvānarī concentration (*dhāraṇā*), which always effects mastery over fire.

That which resembles a heap of powdered collyrium, situated between the two eyebrows, consisting of wind and accompanied by the syllable *ya*, where the Lord (Īśvara) is the presiding deity—having restrained the vital breath there for five ghaṭikās, one should maintain it with the mind; this is the Vāyavī Dhāraṇā, which enables the practitioners of self-restraint to travel through the sky.
The ether, which resembles perfectly pure water, resides in the *brahma-randhra*; there, together with the primordial Sadāśiva, is the peaceful syllable *Ha*.

Having restrained the vital breath (*prāṇa*) there for five *ghaṭikās*, one should hold it along with the mind. This is declared to be the "ether-concentration" (*nabho-dhāraṇā*), which is skillful in splitting open the door to liberation.
The immobilizing, the liquefying, the burning, the bewildering,
and likewise the drying— these are the five concentrations (dhāraṇās) regarding living beings.
Having constantly established the five dhāraṇās through action, mind, and speech, the yogi is liberated from all sins. (Gorakṣaśataka 75)
Everything that falls within the range of thought resides in the heart of the yogin;
that state of mind which is certain regarding reality is declared to be meditation (dhyāna). // GorS(1) 76 //
That meditation is of two kinds: with attributes (saguṇa) and likewise without attributes (nirguṇa).
The wise know that which has attributes is distinguished by color, while that which is without attributes is absolute.
The first wheel is the Foundation (ādhāra), resembling molten gold;
by fixing the gaze on the tip of the nose and meditating upon it, one releases all defilements. (Gorakṣaśataka 78)
The second center is Svādhiṣṭhāna, beautifully adorned with a genuine ruby;
by fixing one's gaze on the tip of the nose and meditating [upon it], one is released from sin. (Gorakṣaśataka 79)
Having fixed one's gaze on the tip of the nose and meditated upon the Maṇipūraka wheel, which resembles the rising sun, one may agitate the world.

Having fixed one's gaze on the tip of the nose and meditated upon the power of lightning within the heart-lotus through various types of breath control (prāṇāyāma), one becomes identical with Brahman. (GorS 82)
Having fixed one's gaze on the tip of the nose and meditated upon that which is continuous within the center of the uvula, pure, and born of nectar, one becomes identical with Brahman. (GorS 1.83)
Fixing one's gaze on the tip of the nose and meditating upon the deity situated between the eyebrows, who resembles a smooth pearl, one becomes filled with bliss. (Gorakṣaśataka 84)
Having fixed one's gaze on the tip of the nose and meditated upon Śiva—who is beyond qualities, peaceful, and facing all directions in the sky—one is liberated from suffering. (GorS 1.85)
The anus, the penis, the navel, and the heart-lotus above that;
the uvula, the location of the *lampikā*, and the Supreme Lord between the eyebrows.
Having meditated upon the self as stainless, having the form of space, resembling a mirage or water, and all-pervading, the yogi shall attain yoga. (GorS 87)
Just as these meditation-places for yogins have been described,
when joined with the reality of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi), they bring about the arising of the eight supernatural powers.
Thus, both the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and reality (*tattva*) have been explained. The color is called the adjunct, while the self (*ātman*) is designated as reality. (GorS 1.89)
The limiting adjunct (upādhi) is false cognition; reality remains otherwise [hidden].
For yogins, through constant practice, there occurs the total destruction of all limiting adjuncts. (GorS 1.90)
A crystal gem appears with a distinction according to its own color;
when freed from that distinction of power, it is this very self that is praised. (Gorakṣaśataka 91)
Those who know reality know reality to be free from fear, without support, beyond conceptual proliferation, without dependence, free from affliction, and formless. (Gorakṣaśataka 92)
As long as the five objects, beginning with sound, are perceived within the ears and other sense organs, for that long meditation (dhyāna) is said to exist; beyond that is samādhi.
When the vital breath is completely attenuated and the mind dissolves,
then that state of oneness in equal flavor is designated as samādhi.
Retention (*dhāraṇā*) consists of five *nāḍīs*, meditation (*dhyāna*) consists of sixty *nāḍikās*,
and through twelve days alone, one attains concentration (*samādhi*), which is the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇasaṃyama*). (Gorakṣaśataka 96)
The yogi, disciplined in meditative absorption, perceives neither smell, nor taste, nor form, nor touch, nor sound; he perceives neither self nor other. (GorS 97)
The yogi who is joined with meditative absorption is not devoured by time, is not afflicted by karma, and cannot be overcome by anyone.
Those who know Brahman know Brahman as stainless, immovable, eternal, actionless, devoid of qualities, the great, the consciousness of space, and bliss. (Gorakṣa Śataka 99)
Just as milk is contained in milk, ghee in clarified butter, or fire placed within fire,
the knower of yoga shall eternally attain non-duality in the supreme state.
Like a fire in the forest of the fear of existence, the knower of yoga, by means of the path of the ladder to liberation, shall eternally attain non-duality in the supreme state. *Gorakṣaśataka* 101.
The Gorakṣa-śataka is completed.
